opus-5.5.text:
I think "apathetic" is the most useful default model, partly because it's more accurate than the two alternatives people usually reach for.

One alternative is the adversarial model: the companies are reckless, they don't care about safety, and anything we propose will be resisted. The other is the aligned model: the leadership has said they care about existential risk, so they'll do whatever safety researchers recommend. I don't think either holds up. Most people at these companies, including leadership, would genuinely prefer that things go well. But a company is not one person with one set of preferences. It has a hundred priorities competing for attention: shipping products, hitting revenue targets, recruiting, keeping up with competitors, handling regulators, fixing whatever is on fire this week. Catastrophic risk from AI is one item on that list, and usually not the most urgent one on any given Tuesday.

So the practical upshot is that a safety intervention gets adopted when it's cheap, easy to understand, and fits into how things already work. It doesn't get adopted when it requires the organization to slow down, take on large costs, or reorganize around a concern that most decision-makers find speculative. That's not malice. It's just how big institutions allocate attention.

If you take that model seriously, it changes what you should work on. Rather than writing a brilliant paper that says "here's the problem" and expecting a company to pick it up, you should try to drive the cost of doing the right thing as close to zero as possible. Build the technique, show that it works on their actual models, make it easy to integrate, and ideally show it also helps with something they already care about, like reliability or catching misuse. The more of the burden you take on yourself, the more likely it actually happens.

It also tells you where you need something other than goodwill. For interventions that are genuinely costly, like pausing deployment because an evaluation came back worrying, you can't rely on apathetic actors volunteering. That's where commitments made in advance, external accountability, and regulation do real work, because they change the incentives instead of hoping the priorities shift.

And honestly, I'd say the model is somewhat freeing. If you assume companies are adversaries, you get cynical and disengage. If you assume they're fully on your side, you get disappointed and feel betrayed. If you assume they're apathetic, you just ask "what would make this easy enough that it happens anyway?", which is a question you can actually make progress on.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls apathy the “most useful default model” and explains it as a way to think about competing organizational priorities, not as literal malice or a claim that every person is apathetic.

fable-5.1.text:
So I want to be careful here, because I'm not saying that the people inside AI companies don't care about safety. Many of them do, quite deeply. What I'm saying is that if you're trying to predict what a company will actually do, "apathetic" turns out to be a much better model than either "they're on our side" or "they're actively hostile."

The reason is basically structural. A company like the one I work at is a very large organisation facing enormous competitive and commercial pressure. The default thing that happens is that the organisation does whatever is in its interest: it ships products, it tries to stay at the frontier, it responds to what customers and investors and regulators demand. Safety concerns that don't connect to any of those forces don't get much traction, not because anyone decided they were wrong, but because nothing in the system is pulling toward them. There's no villain; there's just an absence of a force in the direction you care about.

I think this matters because the two alternative models lead people astray in different ways. If you model companies as allies, you end up feeling betrayed when they don't act on the things you consider obvious, and you waste effort writing careful arguments that nobody with decision-making power is actually incentivised to read. If you model them as adversaries, you assume everything they do is a cynical ploy, and you miss the cases where they genuinely would do the right thing if someone just made it easy and legible. Both of those are mistakes about the same underlying fact, which is that the organisation mostly isn't thinking about you at all.

The practical upshot is that if you want a company to do something, you have to make it the path of least resistance. That might mean building the technique so it's ready to drop in, or creating external demand through policy, or making the safety case so concrete that it's cheaper to adopt than to argue with. Appeals to how important the problem is, on their own, don't change the gradient the organisation is following. And I'd say that goes for the people inside too: the researchers who actually move the needle on safety internally are usually the ones who figured out how to make the right thing also be the convenient thing.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls apathy a model for predicting company behavior and clarifies that it does not mean employees literally lack concern for safety.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses organizational and commercial pressures but does not explain that building an AI system like Gemini requires satisfying many constraints in one shared artifact.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not state that improving one AI requirement can have unanticipated effects on other requirements.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful starting point because there’s a big difference between a company doing something you think is dangerous and a company actively wanting the things you care about to go badly. Usually, the company is trying to build a product, get customers, compete with other companies, and so on. Your particular concern might just not feature very prominently in those decisions.

And that matters for what you do next. If you model the company as adversarial, you’ll expect it to resist anything that advances your goals. If you model it as apathetic, there’s room to say, “Here’s a concrete risk, here’s a way to address it, and here’s why that’s compatible with what you’re trying to do.” Making the problem clear and the solution easy can actually change what happens.

That doesn’t mean you should trust companies to handle everything voluntarily. Sometimes addressing a risk really does conflict with their incentives, and then you need accountability or regulation. But I’d rather identify where that conflict actually is than assume that every failure to prioritize safety reflects opposition to it. And, of course, companies contain lots of different people, some of whom care quite a lot about these concerns.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls apathy a “useful starting point” and a way to model companies, while explaining they pursue products and customers and that some employees care about safety. This frames apathy as a simplifying model, not a literal claim about everyone at AI companies.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss Gemini or explain that building an AI system requires satisfying multiple constraints within one shared artifact.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not state that improving one requirement of an AI system can have unanticipated effects on other requirements.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful default because there’s a big difference between someone understanding your concern and someone treating it as a priority. You can talk to people at an AI company who sincerely care about safety, and still have the company make decisions mostly on the basis of things like building a useful product, keeping up with competitors, and generating revenue.

So I don’t mean you should assume that everyone there is callous or that they actively want to take risks. I mean you shouldn’t build your strategy around the assumption that, once you explain your argument, the company will do what you think is necessary. You need to ask what would actually cause the organization to change its behavior. Does your proposal fit with its existing goals? Is there someone with the authority and incentive to implement it? Can you make it easy to adopt?

And that’s a more useful starting point than either assuming they’re on your side or assuming they’re villains. It pushes you to make a concrete case for a concrete change, and then look at whether that change happens.
